author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Choose texture filtering for 2D-heavy PS2 games
summary: Compare fonts, sprites, pixel-art menus, and 3D backgrounds at native output, determine which elements the game expects to be filtered, and keep a per-game choice that avoids both blur and atlas bleeding.
heroAlt: Official PCSX2 capture of a colorful 2D-heavy game scene with sprites, text, and interface artwork

blocks.text: Separate deliberate smoothing from unwanted blur

A 2D-heavy title may mix hand-drawn sprites, pre-rendered backgrounds, scalable polygons, and small fonts in one frame. Nearest sampling can preserve hard sprite pixels but make a deliberately smooth background crawl; forced bilinear filtering can soften text and borrow texels from the next atlas cell. Choose a menu, a dialogue scene, and a gameplay frame containing both 2D and 3D elements so a setting cannot pass by improving only one layer.

Do not use screen magnification alone to decide what the artist intended. Judge normal viewing distance, movement, and a reliable native-output baseline before preferring razor-sharp or fully smoothed edges.

items: A dialogue or inventory screen with small readable text.
A sprite animation against a contrasting background.
A gameplay scene containing a 3D floor or wall.
Native internal resolution with post-sharpening and texture replacement disabled.
Baseline captures under game-controlled or automatic filtering.
1. Cold-boot the menu and capture fonts, icons, selection borders, and background art at native resolution.
2. Record the sprite animation and note whether edge pixels shimmer, blend into the background, or remain stable.
3. Test the emulator's game-controlled/default filtering path first and preserve that capture.
4. Change to the nearest-like or bilinear alternative that the app explicitly supports, modifying no other sampler value.
5. Repeat menu, animation, and 3D gameplay captures at the same camera and UI state.
6. Inspect atlas borders for a one-pixel color line and check whether fonts acquire gray halos.
7. Move to the desired internal resolution and verify that upscaling does not expose neighboring texels.
8. Keep the value only for the verified title; retest separately for another 2D game rather than copying the profile.

blocks.text: The PS2's original sampling rate could hide small gaps and texture-atlas assumptions. Upscaling increases the number of host samples, so filtering that appears harmless at native output may pull invalid neighboring color. Conversely, disabling all filtering can make 3D surfaces and intentionally smoothed artwork unstable. A mixed-layer comparison makes the tradeoff visible.
The chosen mode must preserve legibility, animation, and the title's 3D layer together.

items: Small fonts remain readable without halos or missing strokes.
Sprite silhouettes are stable during animation and do not bleed adjacent atlas colors.
Pre-rendered backgrounds retain intended gradients and detail.
3D surfaces do not gain severe crawl or blocky transitions.
Menus, gameplay, and cutscenes retain the result after a cold boot.
A sprite gains a colored fringe: restore the game-controlled path.
Text becomes crisp only because the complete frame is oversharpened: disable the shader and retest.
One menu improves while gameplay textures break: split the diagnosis instead of forcing a global value.
Artifacts begin only above native resolution: document an upscaling-specific failure boundary.

blocks.text: Set texture filtering back to Automatic or Game-controlled, return to the recorded resolution, disable any comparison shader, and cold-boot the dialogue and gameplay references. Remove the per-game override if it cannot pass all three layer types.
Pixel art does not always mean nearest sampling

Some PS2 art was authored for composite, interlaced, or bilinear presentation and may look harsher on a modern panel. The goal is faithful and stable output, not a rule that every visible pixel must have a hard edge.
